extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, publishers, and editorial staff
extracted.subtask_description: Best-practice guidance for journal editors and publishers on ethical policies and processes for handling submissions, peer review, authorship, conflicts of interest, research integrity, corrections/retractions, and related publication practices. Designed to help editors develop and implement editorial policies and operational procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency — funding disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers have a right to know who funded a research project or the publication of a document; research funders should be listed on all research papers and funding for any type of publication should be stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State sources of funding in the manuscript (including commercial, charity, government); describe the role of the funder in design, recruitment, data collection, analysis, manuscript preparation, and publication decisions unless obvious from contributors; include other support (e.g., OpenAccess fees, editorial assistance) in acknowledgments; encourage inclusion of clinical trial registration numbers when available. Editors should state this requirement in editorial policy and require authors to report funding information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship — accurate attribution and criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The list of authors should accurately reflect who did the work; journal instructions should explain concepts of academic authorship and which contributions qualify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend adopting ICMJE authorship criteria (substantial contributions, drafting/revision, final approval — meeting 1,2 and 3); ask for authorship declarations that all listed authors meet criteria and no qualifying contributors have been omitted; request short descriptions of each author's contributions and whether authors had complete access to data; list non-author contributors and their contributions in acknowledgments. Provide procedures for resolving authorship disputes (explain policy to corresponding author, confirm agreement of all authors before changes; consider publishing corrections if genuine errors). For group authorship, identify individuals taking direct responsibility and list group members in an appendix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collecting authorship information at submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should require authors to submit authorship statements and to decide authorship at study launch where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use submission systems to collect and manage authorship info; ask for statements that all authors meet criteria, no deserving authors omitted, contributors and funding sources acknowledged, and contributors have approved acknowledgments. Policing authorship is beyond the editor's responsibilities, but editors should demand transparent and complete descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior publication / redundant (duplicate) publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals generally consider only work not previously published; authors must declare that submitted work and its essential substance have not been published elsewhere and are not under consideration elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define clearly what is considered prior publication (abstracts and posters usually not considered prior publication); accept translated re-publications only with permissions and clear identification of original source; request copies of related publications if overlap suspected; identify secondary analyses, sub-group analyses and include references/registration numbers to primary sources. If redundancy is discovered after publication, contact authors and consider notice of redundant publication. Provide clear policies on acceptable overlap for non-research pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical trial registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals that publish clinical trials should consider making registration in a public trial registry a requirement before publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage prospective registration at inception using WHO/ICMJE-compliant registries; allow grace periods at editors' discretion for ongoing or recent trials but develop and make clear a policy for trial registration; request trial register name and registration number to appear in the abstract; sample author instruction wording provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling suspected research misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: If editors suspect research misconduct (fabrication, falsification, plagiarism), they should ensure proper investigation by appropriate authorities rather than necessarily investigating themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inform peer reviewers about role in raising concerns; take serious concerns raised by reviewers, allow authors to respond, carry out investigations with speed and due diligence; alert employers, funders, or regulatory authorities as appropriate and encourage their investigation; consult guidance (e.g., ORI Managing Allegations, COPE flowcharts) and follow established flowcharts for fabricated data or plagiarism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protecting rights of research participants and subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should create policies promoting ethical research practices and seek assurances that studies have relevant approvals and informed consent where required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require links to relevant frameworks (e.g., Declaration of Helsinki); ask authors to state approval by ethics committees/IRBs and that experiments had appropriate informed consent; for animal studies include measures to minimize pain and animal care details; reserve right to reject if procedures are doubtful; provide special handling when no local ethics committee exists (explain in article); require explicit consent before publishing identifiable patient information or images except in exceptional public health interest cases with legal counsel; remove identifying information from technical images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informing readers about misconduct — errata, retractions, expressions of concern
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should inform readers if ethical breaches occurred and publish errata, retractions or expressions of concern as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish corrections when errors affect interpretation; publish retractions when work is fraudulent and expressions of concern when suspicions are well-founded; titles should include 'Erratum', 'Retraction', or 'Expression of concern'; publish on numbered pages and list in table of contents; cite the original article and enable readers to understand correction/retraction context; link electronically to original publication and ensure indexing/abstracting services can link errata/retractions to originals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer-review system policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors must ensure peer-review processes are fair, minimize bias, and be explicit about the type of peer review used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a peer-review system (open, single/blind, double-blind, multiple reviewers) suited to the discipline; publish clear policies explaining which types of article are peer reviewed; identify material not peer reviewed; apply consistent standards; maintain confidentiality of communications unless consent or exceptional circumstances apply; ensure editors/board members withdraw from decisions on their own work and have policies for submissions from editorial staff/employees (e.g., special procedures or refusal to consider).

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer reviewer selection and performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors are responsible for ensuring objective, unbiased, and timely peer review by selecting qualified reviewers and monitoring review quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a database of suitably qualified reviewers; monitor and record reviewer quality and timeliness; do not use reviewers who repeatedly produce poor quality, tardy, abusive or unconstructive reviews; ask reviewers to disclose conflicts of interest and to decline if they cannot be fair; consider but do not be bound by authors' suggested reviewers; request notification if reviewers delegate review to staff; follow guidance on reviewer conduct and intellectual property (ORI/Yale 'Ethics of Peer Review').

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of review and publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should aim for timely peer review and publication, particularly when findings may have important implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize papers judged likely to have important implications for priority publication; timing can be affected by themed issues or grouping of submissions; offer online pre-publication (OnlineEarly/OnlineAccepted) to speed access; clearly state expectations for timing in journal policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals process for editorial decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors have a right to appeal editorial decisions and journals should establish and explain mechanisms to handle appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain appeal mechanisms in instructions to discourage unfounded appeals; editors should mediate exchanges between authors and reviewers; if disputes remain, consider inviting additional reviewers; consider stating that the editor's decision following appeal is final; provide processes for others to comment on journal management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicts of interest disclosure policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors, authors, and reviewers must disclose interests that might affect their objectivity, including financial, personal, political, intellectual or religious interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require disclosures from authors and reviewers; define types of conflicts and time period to cover (suggested 3 years); give examples of significance (e.g., small stock holdings vs large consultancy fees) and consider using bands for financial amounts; publish statements describing authors' conflicts or absence thereof when relevant; encourage editors/board/staff to make and update disclosures regularly; when in doubt, disclose. Provide sample wording for disclosures and flowcharts for handling suspected undisclosed conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial independence from owners/publishers
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial independence should be respected; owners/publishers should not interfere with editorial decisions about individual articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set out relationships and principles of editorial independence in formal contracts and establish appeal mechanisms; owners may discuss general policies but must not influence decisions about specific submissions; protect editorial decision-making from sales teams and commercial pressure; if editorial staff have conflicts, deputize decisions to qualified individuals and include a short statement explaining the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial issues and separation of editorial and sales functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial considerations may influence publishing but should not dictate editorial decisions; sales teams must not be involved in editorial decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should judge submissions on scientific merit and minimize commercial influence; if journals publish advertising, sales and editorial functions must be handled separately; inform sales teams about editorial decisions only after decisions are finalized and with agreed limits on information access and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling funded supplements and third-party funded materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals may publish funded supplements or special issues but must ensure funding organisations do not influence selection or editing of content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require that funded material aligns with journal purpose; describe policy for funded items and always present funder names; include declarations of conflicts of interest for authors and editors, acknowledge non-author contributors and their affiliations, describe selection/review/editing processes and how they differ from normal processes; appoint co-editors (one by funder proposer and one by journal) and include a short statement on the editorial process used; funders may choose what to fund but not select authors or control content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and corrections policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors have responsibility to ensure accuracy of published material and to correct errors that could affect interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage authors and readers to report errors; publish corrections distinguishable from retractions and statements of concern; ensure corrections are included in indexing systems and linked to original articles; follow Box 9 guidance for format, citation, electronic linking, and indexing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouraging respectful academic debate
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should encourage correspondence and academic debate while protecting against personal attacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invite authors to respond to correspondence before publication but do not allow authors to veto unfavorable comments; ensure peer-reviewer comments and published correspondence focus on work not the researcher; edit or reject letters containing personal or offensive statements; invite responses and foster constructive debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsible publication practices and sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should pursue suspected misconduct, apply sanctions consistently where misconduct is confirmed, and promote responsible publication practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with authors, journal owners and publishers, and consult COPE, CSE or other bodies for advice; define conditions and processes for imposing and removing sanctions before applying them; consult publisher (e.g., Blackwell) when considering sanctions; encourage adherence to reporting standards (CONSORT, STARD) and professional codes (ICMJE, COPE, ASA, ACS, APA, etc.); provide flowcharts and documented procedures for dealing with ethical problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism and copyright assurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and readers should expect submitted work to be the author's own, not plagiarized, and copyright not breached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require authors to declare work is original and that they own copyright or have permission; enforce via license/assignment forms (Exclusive License Form, OnlineOpen Form, Copyright Assignment Form) submitted before publication; follow transparency and integrity sections when concerns arise; consult publisher FAQs on plagiarism and dual publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual property and copyright licensing policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals must choose a system to protect intellectual property (copyright ownership, licensing, or open access) that fits their purpose and ethos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend systems that license content from authors (e.g., Exclusive License Form) rather than traditional copyright assignment; describe available options (ELF, OOF adhering to Creative Commons, CAF) and ensure legal authority to publish articles; provide links to sample forms and copyright FAQs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer reviewer conduct and confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer reviewers must treat submitted material in confidence and should not steal ideas or plagiarize; journals should set explicit reviewer responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask reviewers to treat manuscripts confidentially and to destroy submitted manuscripts after review; expect allegations of theft/plagiarism to be substantiated and treated seriously; protect reviewers from author contact and discourage direct author–reviewer contact, especially when misconduct is suspected; provide clear reviewer guidelines and consult ORI/Yale 'Ethics of Peer Review'.
